approach_variants.name: Colchuck Lake and the glacier's true-right margin to the lowest point of the buttress
approach_variants.notes:
As for the Colchuck Glacier route: Stuart Lake trailhead, Stuart Lake Trail two and a half miles to the signed fork, right onto the Colchuck Lake Trail and up the switchbacks to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft — about four miles and 2,200 ft, and the last reliable water on the route.

Follow the east-shore boot path to the inlet at the south end, then climb talus and snow up the basin to the toe of the Colchuck Glacier at roughly 6,600-6,800 ft. Instead of continuing toward the col, angle up and across the glacier's true-right margin toward the peak's northeast side.

Cross the moat where snow meets rock — a snow bridge or a wedged block in a good year, and the technical crux of the approach in a lean one. Parties do rope for this.

Given fourteen-plus pitches and a multi-stage approach, most parties either start well before dawn from the car or camp at Colchuck Lake and climb from there. There is no water above the lake.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep for the rock; the moat crossing is easiest early and hardest in a lean year late
hazards: A moat crossing that can be the technical crux of the day in a lean snow year
Two established starts that do not converge until around pitch five
Inconsistent rock — clean crack pitches interspersed with loose, mossy and lichened ground
Loose debris on the long rising ledge traverse, onto anyone below
A long walk-off down the Colchuck Glacier after a fourteen-pitch day
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The buttress is the rock just south of the couloir, and the couloir is the thing you look for first. It is easier to identify a deep slot in a face than a rib on it, so use the Northeast Couloir as your marker and then step south onto the rock beside it. If you are in a narrow snow slot, you are one feature too far north.

Arrival is the lowest point of the rock. The commonly climbed start gains the buttress at its lowest point and heads for wide, broken cracks at about 5.8. Standing at the right place there is nothing lower to climb — the rock runs down into the glacier and the moat, and you had to cross that moat to reach it.

Two starts exist, and mixing them is the routine error here. There is the more travelled version described above and an older, separate start; they do not meet until around the fifth pitch. So a party that steps onto rock wherever the moat happened to be crossable can find itself on neither, on unfamiliar ground, with no way to tell. Cross the moat where it puts you at the lowest rock, not where it is most convenient.

Confirmation in the first two pitches: wide, broken cracks on generally solid rock leading to the crest below a large headwall, then a downclimb of about fifteen feet off the crest before ramps take you up and right. A start with no downclimb in the first few pitches is not this line.

And the bail-out warning: this route has a real reputation for parties retreating because they cannot find the crux dihedral higher up. If the base was ambiguous, the rest of the day will be worse.
